extracted.intended_audience: citizens, stakeholders, students and practitioners interested in U.S. federal rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the issuance and public-comment process for a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) in U.S. administrative law, including legal requirements, required contents of a notice, comment periods, and exceptions/procedural variants (NOI/ANPRM/FNPRM).

rubrics_metrics.name: APA §553 publication requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal agencies are required to publish NPRMs before finalizing regulations, as required by section 553 of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not a Constitutional requirement, Congress created this requirement to inform affected persons and force agencies to listen to comments and concerns of people likely affected by the regulation. Some emergency rulemakings may bypass the NPRM process (see emergency exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical public comment period length
rubrics_metrics.description: An NPRM is typically published in the Federal Register and allows 60 days for public comment and an additional 30 days for reply comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original comments may still be filed within the reply-comments time window. This is the normal method, but agencies may vary timing for specific proceedings or emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content: statement of time, place, and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Each notice must include a statement of the time, place, and nature of the proposed rulemaking proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This informs interested persons when and how the proceeding will occur (e.g., public hearings, submission deadlines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content: reference to authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Each notice must include a reference to the authority under which it is issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifying statutory or regulatory authority grounds the agency's power to propose the rule and helps commenters target legal arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content: description of subjects, issues, or substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Each notice must include a description of the subjects and issues involved or the substance and terms of the proposed regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description should give sufficient detail about the proposal's scope and specific regulatory text or substantive changes so commenters can provide informed input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content: statement of comment submission deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Each notice must include a statement of the time within which written comments must be submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets the official comment window and enables administrative record management; agencies typically state both initial comment and reply-comment deadlines when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content: statement of participation opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Each notice must include a statement of how and to what extent interested persons may participate in the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covers options such as written comments, public hearings, electronic submission through portals (e.g., Regulations.gov), and any limitations on participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of NOI / ANPRM for preliminary input
rubrics_metrics.description: An NPRM may be preceded by a Notice of Inquiry (NOI) or an Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) in which comments are invited but no rules have yet been proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary comments and data received during this phase allow the agency to prepare a more informed NPRM; agencies use NOIs/ANPRMs to solicit background information and options before drafting regulatory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Further NPRM (FNPRM) when proposal changes drastically
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may publish a 'Further notice of proposed rulemaking' (FNPRM) after an NPRM if comments lead the agency to change the proposal drastically such that further comment is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency's revisions materially alter the proposal, issuing an FNPRM restarts the public-comment opportunity on the revised proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency rulemaking disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA allows for emergency rulemakings that may bypass the NPRM process; when an agency bypasses NPRM it must disclose its reason when publishing the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies invoking emergency procedures should explain the factual and legal basis for the bypass in the final rule to justify departing from normal notice-and-comment procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service-based exception to Federal Register publication
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain cases a notice is not required to be published in the Federal Register if all persons subject to it are named and personally served with a copy of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrow exception applies where direct personal service reaches all affected parties; agencies should ensure adequate service to rely on this exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling and continuing-proceeding notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules are labeled as 'Final rule' in some agencies, or 'Report and order' (R&O) in others; agencies may publish additional R&O notices when conducting a continuing proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different agencies use different nomenclature for final actions; continuing proceedings (e.g., multi-step transitions) can generate multiple notices reflecting stages of the docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Regulations.gov for public access and submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government established Regulations.gov to provide better public access to the rulemaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations.gov serves as a central portal for publishing NPRMs and receiving public comments, increasing accessibility and transparency for stakeholders.
